On Sunday, the New York Yankees will finish their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix.
They are coming off a 5-3 loss on Saturday night.
That said, the series is tied up at 1-1 heading into the finale.
George Lombard Jr. Makes Honest Gerrit Cole Statement
On Friday, Gerrit Cole got the start.
He allowed just two earned runs in 6.0 innings.
After the game, George Lombard Jr. was asked about Cole (via YES Network).
Reporter: “Gerrit won a Cy Young in 2023 when you graduated from high school. What’s it like for you to play behind him?”
Lombard Jr.: “It’s awesome. Yeah. I’ve watched him dominate on the mound for as long as I can remember. It’s really cool to be on the same field as him.”
Looking At Lombard Jr.
Lombard Jr. was picked in the 1st round of the 2023 MLB Draft.
He made his MLB debut last month.
The 21-year-old is currently batting .227 with 29 hits, four home runs, 15 RBIs, 19 runs and two stolen bases in 36 games.
Looking At Cole
Cole has been one of the best pitchers in the recent era of baseball.
The former Cy Young Award winner is in the middle of his 6th season pitching for New York.
He has also had stops with the Houston Astros and Pittsburgh Pirates.
Right now, Cole is 9-9 with a 3.63 ERA in 21 starts.
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 89-65 record in 154 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games (and are 47-33 in 80 games on the road).
On Tuesday, the Yankees will return home to host the Tampa Bay Rays in the Bronx.

PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.
Making matters tougher is that the Rays, owners of the AL’s best record, currently lead the season series between the two teams, 6-3. There’s also the fact that the Yankees will be without Aaron Judge, who returned to the injured list with calf strain on Saturday.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball, so it’s tough to climb up in the standings when they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said after going 0-for-4 on Saturday. “So mathematically, it’s pretty tough, but gotta keep on rolling.”
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough,” added Cam Schlittler, who allowed one earned run over six innings but committed a costly error on Saturday. “I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
The good news for the Yankees is that their best starters are lined up to face the Rays. While they haven’t officially announced their probables for the series, it looks like Max Fried and Carlos Rodón will pitch the doubleheader before Gerrit Cole and Schlittler, the Cy Young frontrunner, close out the four-game set.
The Rays, however, are set to throw a few of their best with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez, Ian Seymour and Freddy Peralta slotted for the highly-anticipated matchup.
While they’re not officially out of the division race yet, the likeliest scenario is that the Yankees end up hosting Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year. It is not where the team wants to end up after finishing 2025 with the same record as the Blue Jays but losing the season series tiebreaker, but Bellinger remained confident that the Yankees can still win their first title since 2009.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off days,” he said. “That’s always goal No. 1. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card.”

The New York Yankees fell in heartbreaking fashion on Saturday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers, losing on a walk-off two-run shot from Pavin Smith.
New York is now 89-65 on the season and still sits firmly in the top Wild Card spot but trails the Tampa Bay Rays by five games for the AL East division.
Currently, the biggest concern for the Yankees stems from injuries, as Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. are all sidelined. Even rookie slugger Spencer Jones seems to be dealing with some type of foot injury.
Aaron Boone Makes Statement on Jones’ Decision
Fortunately, Jones’ injury does not seem serious as he said pregame it was “no big deal.”
In fact, Boone said that he was available off the bench during Saturday night’s game and ultimately explained why he didn’t use him as a pinch-hitter.
After a reporter asked Boone if Jones was available or if he was trying to stay away from him because of the injury, Boone made it clear that he would’ve gone to him if the right spot emerged.
“He was available, like I would’ve… if a spot came up to hit or we needed to do something I would’ve gone to him,” Boone said.
Aaron Boone speaks to the media following the Yankees 5-3 loss tonight in Arizona. pic.twitter.com/aeBBxybvHN
— YES Network (@YESNetwork) September 20, 2026
Looking at the Yankees
New York will play the Diamondbacks one more time on Sunday and then, after a day off Monday, will begin a massive four-game set with the Rays. If they can sweep the series, they could get back into the race over the final three games of the regular season.
On Tuesday, the two teams will play a doubleheader and then wrap it up across Wednesday and Thursday, with the Yankees likely throwing their top four guys in Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, Gerrit Cole, and Cam Schlittler.

Second year pitcher Cam Schlittler is the strong American League Cy Young candidate, but he may have a chance at another award. The New York Yankees ace continues to add to the great body of work and saw his ERA dropping below 2.00 in recent weeks. Schlittler has an outside chance at the AL MVP Award since he's arguably the best player in the entire MLB right now.ESPN's Bradford Doolittle uses an advanced stats model, and it recently saw Schlittler moving up in the rankings via his AXE rating:
"Front-runner: Yordan Alvarez, Astros (146.9 AXE). Next: 2, Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees (143.0).
Schlitter has an uphill battle, but if I'd included pitchers in the MVP tables earlier, he would have been a fixture all season. Now he's earning a little buzz both in articles speculating on awards consideration and the betting markets. I don't think he'll win, but for a 2026 starting pitching to get so prominently mentioned, that tells you all you need to know about how dynamic he has been."
Doolittle confirmed that he expects Houston Astros slugger Alvarez to win the award since it's extremely difficult for pitchers to take home MVP. However, he made sure to note that Schlittler making this race at all shows he's having a historically great season for the contending Yankees roster.
How Cam Schlittler Can Win The MVP
Alvarez remains the strong favorite to win the AL MVP, but his Astros are still battling to make the playoffs. Houston is currently tied for first place in the American League West with the Texas Rangers both having 77-77 records. Voters could punish Alvarez for team success if the Astros miss the playoffs and finish with a record under .500. Schlittler must hope for some luck of Houston failing and finishing his season strong with the Yankees having the second-best American League record. An important start against the Tampa Bay Rays could see Schlittler having a "statement performance" if it helps the Yankees have a chance at the AL East title. Hitters getting the advantage in MVP voting requires Schlittler to finish perfectly to have a viable shot.
Current Betting Odds Hurt Cam Schlittler
Doolittle's model is fully based off advanced stats, and fan discussions do little to help Schlittler's case with baseball media. Current betting odds on various sports gambling sites see Schlittler still distantly behind Alvarez and Junior Caminero. Bet MGM has the following odds for viable American League MVP candidates, as of September 19, 2026;
Alvarez: -2000
Caminero: +1100
Schlittler: +6000
Unfortunately for the Yankees and Schlittler, the odds show that it may be too late for him to make up ground in the narratives. Alvarez has been considered the favorite since he started putting up strong slugging numbers early in the season. Schlittler should take pride in likely winning the Cy Young Award and even creating enough momentum to get any MVP consideration as a pitcher in 2026. The postseason will see Schlittler hoping to lead a rotation with Gerrit Cole and Max Fried to the World Series.

Los New York Yankees respondieron con autoridad en su primer partido sin Aaron Judge y derrotaron 9-2 a los Arizona Diamondbacks este viernes en Chase Field. Nueva York fabricó cinco carreras en la primera entrada, Ben Rice y George Lombard Jr. conectaron cuadrangulares y Gerrit Cole lanzó seis entradas de calidad para llevarse una victoria que también tuvo un significado histórico para el derecho.

La jornada comenzó con una noticia importante para los Yankees: Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Sin su principal figura ofensiva, Nueva York necesitó encontrar producción desde el primer turno y la respuesta llegó inmediatamente frente al abridor de Arizona, Eduardo Rodríguez.
Los primeros cinco bateadores de los Yankees lograron embasarse. Ben Rice recibió una base por bolas y posteriormente Amed Rosario conectó un sencillo productor para abrir la pizarra. Después llegaron más oportunidades para la ofensiva neoyorquina, hasta que George Lombard Jr. conectó un sencillo de dos carreras que llevó el marcador a 5-0 antes de que terminara el primer episodio. Rodríguez necesitó 45 lanzamientos para conseguir los tres outs de la entrada, la mayor cantidad de su carrera en un primer inning.
Arizona intentó reaccionar en el segundo capítulo. Corbin Carroll conectó un cuadrangular de dos carreras para acercar a los Diamondbacks a 5-2 y darle algo de vida al público de Chase Field. Sin embargo, Cole logró contener la ofensiva local y evitó que la reacción se transformara en una amenaza mayor.
La respuesta de los Yankees llegó en la tercera entrada. Ben Rice volvió a aparecer y conectó un cuadrangular solitario, su número 39 de la temporada, para recuperar la diferencia de cuatro carreras y colocar el encuentro 6-2. El batazo también completó una noche ofensiva sobresaliente para Rice, quien terminó con dos imparables, dos bases por bolas, dos carreras y dos carreras impulsadas.
Mientras la ofensiva seguía produciendo, Cole encontró estabilidad desde la lomita. Después del cuadrangular de Carroll, el derecho no permitió otra carrera y completó seis entradas con cuatro hits, dos carreras limpias, ninguna base por bolas y seis ponches. Venía de dos aperturas en las que había permitido siete jonrones combinados, por lo que su actuación en Phoenix representó una recuperación importante en su temporada.
Lombard Jr. volvió a aparecer en la sexta entrada. El campocorto conectó su tercer jonrón de la temporada, esta vez solitario, para ampliar la ventaja de Nueva York a 7-2. El joven infielder terminó la noche con dos imparables y tres carreras impulsadas, convirtiéndose en otra de las figuras ofensivas del triunfo visitante.
Ver esta publicación en Instagram
Los Yankees agregaron dos carreras más en la séptima entrada para terminar de sentenciar el encuentro. La ofensiva visitante terminó con ocho hits y nueve carreras, mientras que Arizona consiguió siete imparables, pero no volvió a pisar el plato después del segundo inning.
Para Cole, la victoria tuvo un valor especial. El derecho llegó a 162 triunfos en su carrera, superando a Mike Moore y convirtiéndose en el lanzador con más victorias entre los jugadores que fueron seleccionados con el primer pick global del Draft. Cole fue elegido por los Pittsburgh Pirates con la primera selección en 2011.
La derrota, en cambio, complicó todavía más el panorama de Arizona en la recta final de la temporada. Los Diamondbacks llegaron al encuentro buscando mantenerse en la pelea por el último boleto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, pero la caída ante Nueva York significó su tercera derrota consecutiva. Al término de la jornada quedaron cinco juegos por detrás del último puesto de Wild Card, con ocho encuentros restantes.
Los Yankees, ya clasificados a los playoffs, mejoraron a 89-64 y se colocaron a cuatro juegos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con nueve partidos por disputar. Nueva York además consiguió su octava victoria en sus últimos 10 encuentros.
El triunfo llegó, además, en una noche en la que los Yankees tuvieron que afrontar la ausencia de Judge. Rice y Lombard Jr. aportaron los batazos largos, mientras que Cole respondió desde el montículo para que Nueva York tomara el primer partido de la serie en Arizona con una victoria contundente de 9-2.

Last night was a good night for the Yankees, seeing the team put up five runs in the first paired with a good Gerrit Cole outing to cruise to a 9-2 win over the Diamondbacks. The club also picked up a game on the Rays as the AL East leaders dropped the opener of their series to the Red Sox. Tonight, the Yankees have two goals: get the win to stay in a hypothetically-competitive division race (all but necessary since Tampa Bay avenged the loss with a 2-1 win over Boston this afternoon), and build out a little more breathing room in the Cy Young race.
Dylan Cease had his worst start of the year on Friday for the Blue Jays, going just 2.2 innings and walking six. He and today's Yankee starter Cam Schlittler have had a heavyweight bout atop the Cy leaderboard all year, and while Cam's pulled away a bit in recent weeks, he can start to put the finishing touches on his case tonight. He hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start since August 3rd (!!), making us all maybe expect a bit too much from the righty who can seemingly do no wrong. Schlittler has thrown 45 innings across those aforementioned seven starts, so he's not a five-and-fly guy, and his 1.00 ERA in that stretch is just…a farce.
Brandon Pfaadt is having the best season of his young career, with a 3.77 ERA and 4.06 FIP that are both significant steps forward after a pretty lost 2025. He doesn't strike many men out though, and a 45 percent ground ball rate means heavy sinking fastballs in the zone. There will be pitches to hit from Pfaadt; you just need to be able to elevate them.
Ben Rice had himself a fantastic game cleaning up last night and is bumped up to the leadoff spot tonight, with
Luis García Jr. getting the nod over Paul Goldschmidt at first base. Spencer Jones reportedly has a sore left foot, which means we get José Caballero in center, and I'm going to withhold comment on that decision for now.
It's an 8:10pm Eastern start but not a national broadcast, this one's on YES. The Diamondbacks will be celebrating their 2001 World Series championship throughout the evening, which seems kind of lame because you can't really "win" a championship when you didn't have an opponent.

PHOENIX — Without any guarantees of it happening, Aaron Judge is holding out hope of returning from a calf strain in time for the playoffs.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason; that’s definitely the plan,” Judge said Saturday afternoon. “We’re going to do everything we can to get back as soon as we can.”
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
That was a slightly less definitive statement than what Judge consistently said during the summer when he was trying to come back from a right rib stress fracture, which he did after three-plus months on Sept. 8.
But now the clock is ticking even louder, with Saturday marking 10 days away from Game 1 of the American League wild card series.
“Definitely frustrated,” said Judge, who played seven games after missing 84 on the IL with the rib injury. “Dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult.”
Judge did not reveal what grade the strain was, but said it involved his Soleus muscle, which he indicated was more important to running and hitting compared to the gastrocnemius muscle.
“The focus is still the same, to be ready to go for October,” Judge said.
In the meantime, the Yankees are banking on their summer without Judge paying off now that he is back on the IL.
“Lean on each other,” Cody Bellinger said. “The game itself is hard; if you add too much pressure on yourself, the game becomes even harder. So we really just have to play for each other, lean on each other, pass the baton, do your job and control what you can control.”
The Yankees did that on Friday night, racing out of the gates to score five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 win against the Diamondbacks, just hours after the team announced Judge was going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain.
But they also got off well at the beginning of June after Judge landed on the IL with a right rib stress fracture before their lineup became a black hole for an extended stretch during the summer. They had finally started to break out of it shortly before Judge got back on Sept. 8, but after having him back for seven games, they now find themselves in the same spot again, less than two weeks away from the start of the playoffs.
“We’ve played most of the year this way, and I feel like in a lot of cases, especially some of our key guys over the last few weeks have started to, especially offensively, get it going like we know they’re capable of,” manager Aaron Boone said.
During the 84-game span that Judge missed this summer, the Yankees ranked 26th in runs per game (4.06), 29th in batting average (.227), 27th in OPS (.681), and 29th in WRC+ (90).
But over the tail end of that stretch, and into Judge’s return, the Yankees started to hit more like they are capable of. That included the trade deadline addition of Luis García Jr., the emergence of rookie outfielder Spencer Jones, and Bellinger getting back on track after returning from his own hamstring injury in August.
Perhaps most importantly, it has coincided with the reemergence of Ben Rice. The lefty slugger was a game wrecker for the first two months of the season before Judge went down, then cooled off a bit during the summer (albeit with some good stretches along the way) before catching fire again over the last few weeks. Entering Saturday, over his last 22 games, Rice had hit .353 with a 1.037 OPS and five home runs, including his 39th of the season Friday night.
“Special year,” Gerrit Cole said. “Has made some really good adjustments from previous years, going into this year, and I think he’s really started to heat back up here the last few weeks after having to make some adjustments in the middle of the season. Not only is he really proficient with the bat, but he’s a smart player and a hard worker, which is leading him to have a really outstanding season for us.”
The Yankees need that to continue for however long Judge is out (and even if and when he returns) for them to play deep into October, though Rice isn’t looking at it as having to do any more — which got some hitters in trouble during the three-time AL MVP’s first absence.
“I would think that everyone just goes out there and stays within themselves, tries to put together quality at-bat after quality at-bat,” he said. “Pitching is always going to be doing their thing, like they have for us all year. So from an offensive standpoint, just do what we did [Friday]: go out and have a team at-bat, trust the guy behind you and keep the line moving.”
To Rice’s point, the Yankees have leaned on the strength of their pitching staff all season, but that was especially the case during Judge’s three months on the IL this summer, when they were able to scratch out enough wins in low-scoring games, with their pitchers keeping them in it almost every night.

We have a lot of perfectionists in here. We’re always striving to be perfect and trying to be the best. But the reality is we’ve had a lot of obstacles we’ve had to overcome and, by and large, we’ve played really well.”

Returning to the mound after missing an entire regular season due to an elbow injury is a daunting task for any pitcher. That context helps explain why Gerrit Cole endured a slow start to his 2026 campaign upon returning to the New York Yankees‘ rotation.
However, Cole’s recent surge on the bump has generated plenty of momentum within the organization. When asked whether the veteran righty would take the ball in the Wild Card round, manager Aaron Boone delivered a resolute answer: “I would expect Gerrit Cole to start, yes.”
Boone faces a compelling rotational dilemma, given the standout performances of his depth chart. Max Fried has anchored his share of gems, while breakout starter Cam Schlittler has delivered a dominant campaign, one that Boone firmly believes warrants American League Cy Young honors.
With Aaron Judge sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, the Yankees are relying heavily on their pitching depth to carry the load into October. That group could get another boost with Ryan Weathers tracking toward a postseason return.

Cole’s rollercoaster season
Cole’s season started with immediate frustration before he ever threw an official pitch. Lingering elbow concerns during Spring Training delayed his season debut, forcing him to miss the opening two months of the championship schedule and putting extra stress on the Yankees‘ starting rotation.
Dominant, double-digit strikeout performances—including a 10-strikeout shutout performance over 6.2 innings against Kansas City and multi-hit gems against Chicago and Atlanta—showed he remains one of the most electric arms in baseball.
A recurring issue throughout Cole’s 2026 campaign has been his home run rate. When Cole misses over the plate, opposing hitters have made him pay, elevating his HR/9 rate above his career averages and making several of his outings much more high-stress than his strikeout numbers would indicate.

Cam Schlittler has all but wrapped up the American League Cy Young Award.
The Pinstriped phenom is a -25000 favorite to become the seventh Yankee to win the honor at bet365 Sportsbook, and the biggest prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket, have him priced at 96 percent. There are no sure things in baseball nor in betting, but this one is pretty darn close.
While Schlittler will be making room for at least one award this winter, a debate has begun to spark up about whether the 25-year-old should also garner heavy consideration for another: AL MVP.
No pitcher has won the award in either league since Clayton Kershaw did so for the Dodgers in 2014.
Kershaw’s stat line that season was impeccable. He went 21-3, pitched to a 1.77 ERA and 0.86 WHIP, and racked up 239 strikeouts against just 31 walks in 198 1/3 innings. By season’s end, the future Hall-of-Famer had a WAR of 8.2.
Plenty has changed in baseball in the 12 years since Kershaw dominated the league, but Schlittler’s resume pops just as much. He leads the league in innings pitched, ERA, WHIP, and scoreless starts, and he’s second in strikeouts and quality starts. His 5.9 WAR at FanGraphs lags behind just Kansas City’s Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Houston’s Yordan Alvarez (6.0) in the American League.
Alvarez, who was a Triple Crown threat for much of the year, is the -4000 favorite to be named AL MVP. Schlittler is currently priced at 50/1 at bet365 Sportsbook, making him the third-favorite, sandwiched between Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero and Witt Jr.
Caminero, who leads the American League with 41 home runs, is 14/1. Witt is 125/1.
Those odds suggest that the race is over. At -4000, Alvarez owns a 97.6-percent implied probability. Kalshi has it a shade lower at 89 percent. If that was the case, why did the Schlitter-for-MVP talks get so loud that his teammates shared their thoughts?
The answer is because the right-hander has a legitimate claim to the award. Not only by the numbers, but also by the literal meaning of the award. Who was the most valuable player to his team in 2026?
With Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon all injured for large chunks of the season, Schlittler was the only Yankee starter that Aaron Boone was able to send out every five days. He took that responsibility head-on in his second season in the majors, delivering a 1.95 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, and 228 strikeouts in 184 2/3 innings so far.
Without that level of dominance, the Yankees could be scrapping for a wild-card spot; instead, they’re still in the hunt for the best record in the American League.
Schlittler has two starts remaining, likely against the Diamondbacks on Saturday and a potentially massive one versus the Rays on Thursday. If he is able to replicate what he did in his most recent outing against the Mets in those final two appearances, he’ll have plenty of voters thinking long and hard about whether he deserves this award.
At 50/1 odds this late in the season, it’s a chance worth taking.

item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

Gerrit Cole's two-game stretch against the San Diego Padres and the New York Mets raised concerns. With the postseason weeks away for the New York Yankees, Cole, who should be their two starter heading into the postseason, allowed seven home runs and nine earned runs in 11.1 IP. It was a ghastly set of performances, and it may have left the organization wondering how the rest of the season would shake out for their former Cy Young winner.
If there were any questions about Cole's abilities, his start against the 80-74 Arizona Diamondbacks may have alleviated a few worries. It may also have put to rest any internal debates. Cole did allow a home run this time out, but it was just one. Corbin Carroll pulled a 388-foot home run off Cole's bat at 110.7 MPH.
Headed into the postseason, pitching in Game 1 is an easy decision. Aaron Boone needs to hand the ball to Cy Young frontrunner and prospective MVP candidate Cam Schlittler. There's no reason to really overthink that one.
If Cole starts struggling again, though, the question of who the second starter is gets a little trickier. That might still be a conversation worth having if things go differently to close out the year, but for now, if Cole pitches the way he did against the Diamondbacks, there's no reason to save him for another series.
Cole's big test will be against the Tampa Bay Rays, since he lines up to face them in their next series. If he pitches well against them, he'll further solidify his spot as the team's two-starter.
A better outing for Gerrit Cole
When Aaron Boone was asked about Cole after the game, he said he wasn't too worried. He chalked his struggles up to a long season.
"I think a lot of people probably overreacted to a couple of outings that, frankly, are inevitable in a long season," Boone said, according to the New York Post's Greg Joyce. "The reality is he's having an outstanding season, he's throwing the ball really well, and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments when you have a couple where they get to you."
The Carroll blast was Cole's lone blemish. He pitched six innings of two-run ball, striking out six, allowing no walks, and four hits.
On the back end, he gave up a ton of soft contact. The Diamondbacks had an average exit velocity of 86.8 MPH against him. That's way down from his last two starts, when batters averaged 96.8 MPH against him.
This is the type of Cole the Yankees need in the postseason. Who knows what's happening with Aaron Judge, so the rotation and bullpen have to essentially be perfect if this team is going to make any noise this postseason.

For a historic franchise like the New York Yankees, rotation stability is paramount over the long haul of a 162-game season. That makes Cam Schlittler’s dominant breakout campaign all the more remarkable—so much so that manager Aaron Boone believes the young right-hander has built a compelling case to take home the American League Cy Young Award.
When asked about Schlittler’s transformative presence in the rotation, Boone didn’t mince words: “Well, he’s gonna win the Cy Young!” The manager’s ringing endorsement underscores just how dominant Schlittler has been on the mound this year.
While Boone continues to navigate rotation depth with Ryan Weathers sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, Schlittler gives the Yankees a legitimate ace to rely on as they gear up for October.
On the offensive side, Boone is also monitoring the return timeline for slugger Aaron Judge, who was sidelined with a calf strain. In the meantime, the Yankees skipper has relied on depth options like Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger to keep the lineup producing.
Key milestones driving Schlittler’s Cy Young case
A stellar 2026 breakout campaign with the Yankees has vaulted Schlittler directly into the front-runner conversation for the American League Cy Young Award. Stepping up as the de facto ace while Gerrit Cole missed time, Schlittler has delivered elite run suppression, swing-and-miss stuff, and exceptional durability.
Here is a breakdown of the key numbers and milestones anchoring Schlittler’s Cy Young candidacy:
- 1.95 ERA: Schlittler took over the MLB ERA lead in September, standing as the only qualified starter with an ERA under 2.00.
- Historical run: His 1.71 ERA through his first 16 starts marked the lowest ERA by a Yankees starter through that stretch since Hall of Famer Whitey Ford in 1964.
- 228 Strikeouts in 184.2 IP (11.1 K/9): Schlittler eclipsed the 200-strikeout mark on August 28 against Boston, becoming the fourth-youngest pitcher in franchise history to achieve the feat.
- Signature outings: Highlighted by a career-high 13-strikeout performance against the Cincinnati Reds on June 19, along with double-digit strikeout shutouts against Philadelphia (12 K) and Atlanta (11 K).
Other top Cy Young contenders
Schlittler isn’t running unopposed in a tightly contested American League race. Strong campaigns from power arm Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and left-hander Garrett Crochet of the Boston Red Sox keep them firmly in the mix.
Over in the National League, the Cy Young field features plenty of heavy hitters, headlined by Milwaukee Brewers phenom Jacob Misiorowski, Atlanta Braves veteran Chris Sale, and the Philadelphia Phillies duo of Cristopher Sanchez and Jesus Luzardo.

New York Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole still has a very big problem heading into the MLB playoffs.
Cole allowed four hits while registering six strikeouts, and his control remained sharp without any walks. He did surrender yet another home run, but for the most part, this was a solid outing by the right-hander.
Cole generated just six swings-and-misses on 62 strikes against the Diamondbacks, marking a 15 percent whiff rate. And while that was better than his eight percent rate against the New York Mets in his preceding start, it's still not good.
In fact, on the season as a whole, Cole has posted a 21.3 percent whiff rate, which places him in the 18th percentile in baseball.
Cole has been declining in that area for quite some time now, but this season has been particularly bad in that department.
Now, thanks to Cole's pinpoint control and his ability to paint corners, he still owns a 9.1 K/9 rate this year, a testament to just how good of a pitcher he is.
And while his average fastball velocity (96.8 mph) still ranks in the 85th percentile, his secondary stuff is simply not as lethal anymore.
Cole has still managed to log a 3.63 ERA in spite of his question marks this season, but the days of him being a bona fide ace appear to be over.
It also begs the question of whether or not he would be the Yankees' best option for a No. 2 starter in the playoffs. We know that Cam Schlittler will be the lead arm. But will Cole get the nod over Max Fried? An argument can even be made for Carlos Rodon, who has been very good when healthy this season.
Chances are, Aaron Boone will hand the No. 2 job to Cole because he's Gerrit Cole and because he has been good for most of 2026. But the fact that Cole's stuff is clearly declining — and right before the postseason — is a major concern.
Cole is smart enough where he can find ways to work around his ace stuff no longer being there. We just saw it in Arizona on Friday night. But can the Yankees trust him enough at this stage to get a pivotal Game 2 start?
We're about to find out.

PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler llega este sábado al Chase Field con otra oportunidad de convertir una temporada que ya es dominante en algo aún más difícil de alcanzar para el resto de la Liga Americana.
El lanzador diestro de los Yankees llega a su partido contra Arizona con un balance de 14-6, una efectividad de 1,95, un WHIP de 0,90 y 228 strikeouts en 184 2/3 entradas. Ha cedido una carrera o menos en siete salidas seguidas, una racha que le ha llevado de ser un simple aspirante a situarse en el centro de las conversaciones sobre el premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, mientras que los Yankees se han asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada.
El contraste con su rival más cercano se acentuó el viernes por la noche sin que Schlittler lanzara ni una sola bola. El as de Toronto, Dylan Cease , solo aguantó 2 2/3 entradas en la derrota por 7-1 ante Texas. Concedió seis bases por bolas, encajó cuatro carreras (solo una limpia) y solo 36 de sus 74 lanzamientos fueron strikes. Sportsnet también midió su bola rápida a 93,6 mph, 3,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Cease sigue teniendo una temporada de élite. Tras la derrota, tiene un balance de 11-6, con una ERA de 2,40, un WHIP de 1,10 y 239 strikeouts en 169 entradas, lo que le sitúa a la cabeza de la Liga Americana. Su total de ponches sigue siendo mejor que el de Schlittler. Sin embargo, su promedio de carreras limpias, la eficiencia en su carga de trabajo y su control reciente marcan ahora un contraste estadístico más marcado, justo en el momento en que las opiniones sobre los premios se van consolidando.
Para los Yankees, eso va más allá de los trofeos. Schlittler se ha convertido en el miembro más estable de un cuerpo de lanzadores de los Yankees que ha tenido que lidiar con las ausencias de Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón. Además, está previsto que sea el primero en lanzar en la rotación de Nueva York en octubre, lo que hace que sus últimas salidas en la temporada regular cobren importancia tanto para la lucha por los playoffs como para la carrera por los premios.
Los Yankees llegan al sábado con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay, así que cada salida que le queda sigue teniendo un interés inmediato más allá de la carrera por los premios.
Una votación unánime cambia el panorama de la carrera
Esta semana ha llegado la señal más clara hasta ahora. En la última votación del premio Cy Young de la temporada en MLB.com, los 32 votantes eligieron al as de los Yankees como el número uno de la Liga Americana. Consiguió el máximo de 160 puntos. Cease quedó segundo con 126.
El jurado pidió a los votantes que clasificaran a cinco lanzadores en una escala del 5 al 1 (5-4-3-2-1), teniendo en cuenta tanto lo que había pasado como cómo podrían desarrollarse las dos últimas semanas. Esa distinción es importante. La encuesta no es la votación oficial de la BBWAA y no decide el premio, pero la unanimidad entre los 32 votantes de MLB.com muestra lo mucho que ha subido la posición del as de los Yankees.
El último modelo de premios de ESPN apunta en la misma dirección. Su sistema AXE sitúa a Schlittler en primer lugar entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con 153,1, por delante de Cease, que tiene 145,8. ESPN señaló que Schlittler ya llevaba un balance de 12-6 con una efectividad de 2,09 hasta agosto, y que luego empezó septiembre con un 2-0 y una efectividad de 0,89 en sus tres primeras salidas del mes.
El caso de Cone explica por qué los números tienen más peso
David Cone ha definido el valor de Schlittler basándose en algo más sencillo que una fórmula para los premios. El exganador del premio Cy Young de los Yankees destacó la constancia con la que este lanzador diestro ha aliviado la presión de anotar sobre la alineación y el bullpen.
«¿Dónde estarían los Yankees sin él?», dijo Cone.
A continuación, Cone situó a Schlittler al mismo nivel que las estrellas más valiosas de la liga al hablar de lo mucho que Nueva York ha dependido de él a lo largo de una temporada marcada por los cambios constantes en la rotación.
«Schlittler está entre los mejores. Se lo merece, sin duda hay que tenerlo muy en cuenta», dijo Cone.
Ese argumento viene respaldado por la trayectoria de Schlittler esta temporada. Cone señaló esta semana que el lanzador diestro ya había hecho 21 salidas en las que solo había cedido cero o una carrera. En las últimas siete salidas de Schlittler, las estadísticas actuales de la MLB muestran una efectividad de 1,00 en 45 entradas, con 57 ponches y un WHIP de 0,76.
El tropiezo de Cease marca la diferencia en los últimos compases
Lo más revelador es el momento en que se hizo la encuesta. La encuesta de MLB.com se publicó antes de la salida más corta de Cease esta temporada, el viernes en Arlington. Eso significa que el resultado unánime no necesitó su último tropiezo para diferenciar a los dos lanzadores.
Las estadísticas de Cease siguen siendo lo suficientemente buenas como para que la carrera siga siendo reñida. Tiene 11 strikeouts más que Schlittler en 15 2/3 entradas menos. Pero también ha concedido 78 bases por bolas frente a las 44 de Schlittler, y el viernes fue la tercera salida consecutiva en la que Cease no logró completar seis entradas.
Schlittler tendrá la próxima oportunidad de demostrar su valía. Los Yankees lo alinearán contra Brandon Pfaadt el sábado, con Nueva York con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Una buena actuación no garantizaría oficialmente el premio, pero dejaría aún menos margen para que algún rival cambie el panorama de esta recta final de la temporada.
Queda una última prueba antes de octubre
A los Yankees aún les queda más de una semana antes de que termine la temporada regular, y los aficionados de los Yankees saben que las votaciones para los premios no se basan en encuestas de predicción. Una o dos malas salidas finales aún pueden cambiar el panorama. Esa es la incertidumbre que Schlittler debe afrontar.
Lo que ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Schlittler ya no tiene que esforzarse por meterse en la conversación. Las últimas medidas a nivel nacional ya lo han situado al frente, mientras que el mal viernes de Cease ha hecho que la carrera sea aún más dura.
El sábado en Arizona le da al as de los Yankees otra oportunidad de ampliar aún más esa ventaja.

Gerrit Cole has officially added another remarkable accomplishment to his already decorated MLB career. The New York Yankees ace picked up his 162nd career victory Friday night, passing Mike Moore for the most wins ever by a pitcher selected first overall in the MLB Draft.
It is another milestone in what has been a long journey for Cole, who was drafted by the Pittsburgh Pirates, traded to the Houston Astros, and eventually signed with the Yankees.
Cole passes Mike Moore for the record
Jun 9, 2026; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Gerrit Cole (45) reacts in the first inning against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field. Mandatory Credit: David Richard-Imagn Images
Cole reached the milestone during the Yankees' 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks, pitching six strong innings while allowing two runs on four hits with six strikeouts. The win moved him to 162 for his career, one ahead of Moore's 161. David Price ranks third on the list with 157 victories after being selected first overall by Tampa Bay in 2007.
It is a fitting achievement for Cole, who entered professional baseball with enormous expectations after Pittsburgh selected him first overall in 2011 out of UCLA. MLB's official player bio confirms Cole was the Pirates' No. 1 pick that year.
Most wins by a pitcher drafted No. 1 overall:
- Gerrit Cole — 162 wins (2011)
- Mike Moore — 161 wins (1981)
- David Price — 157 wins (2007)
From Pittsburgh to Houston to the Bronx
Cole's path to the record has taken him through three different organizations. The Pirates developed him into a frontline starter before trading him to Houston in January 2018. With the Astros, Cole elevated his game to another level, earning two All-Star selections and finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2019.
He then signed with the Yankees before the 2020 season and eventually won the 2023 AL Cy Young Award. Now, more than 15 years after being selected first overall, Cole owns the record for career victories among pitchers who began their MLB journey with that distinction.

The New York Yankees will play the rest of the regular season without slugger Aaron Judge. While they understand the magnitude of his loss, they enter the stretch run with belief.
The Yanks scored five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the first game of a weekend series Friday, and the teams meet again Saturday in Phoenix as Arizona attempts to stay alive in the National League wild-card race.
"Obviously losing 'Judgey' hurts," Cody Bellinger said. "We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is we're going to have to find a way. The talent in this room speaks for itself.
"I'm fully confident we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody."
American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) will face Arizona right-hander Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) in the second game of the series.
The Diamondbacks (80-74) will ask Pfaadt to end a slump in which they have lost five of six. They are five games behind San Diego, the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots with eight games to play.
"We know where we're at," Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. "We can't afford to worry about things we can't control. I'm going to say there's time. There's always time."
The Yankees (89-64) are 48-39 this season without Judge, who was placed on the injured list Friday with a strained right calf after missing three months earlier with a fractured right rib.
New York is also without injured regulars Jazz Chisholm Jr. (thumb) and Trent Grisham (hamstring), although manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm could return for the Tampa Bay series early next week.
The Yankees, who already have qualified for the postseason, are four games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East, and the teams have a four-game series at Yankee Stadium beginning Tuesday.
"There is no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don't change now," Boone said. "One thing we do know is that we are in the dance.
"We've been built on the strength of our starting pitching all year."
No one has been as strong as Schlittler, who is in his first full season and has made every start while Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon have missed time with injuries or recovery time.
Schlittler has won four of his last five starts and has given up one run or fewer in each of his last seven. He was struck on the back of his right leg by Bo Bichette's 111.5 mph comebacker on his 94th and last pitch of a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets last Sunday, but shrugged it off.
"You have an ace at the top that has pitched like that," Boone said. "That's a good place to start. He's been dominant. This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch last year."
Schlittler has never faced the Diamondbacks, although Jesus Sanchez is 4 for 12 with three walks against him.
Pfaadt is 0-2 with a 5.74 ERA in his last five starts, and he gave up six runs and 10 hits in 6 2/3 innings in a loss to Texas on Aug. 12. He will be pitching on six days' rest after being pushed back so Eduardo Rodriguez could start the first game of the series.
Pfaadt lost his only outing against the Yankees, giving up six runs in 4 1/3 innings of a 7-1 loss as a rookie in 2023. Cody Bellinger is 2 for 7 with two solo homers against him and Luis Garcia Jr. is 3 for 7 with a homer.

item.content:encoded:
For a little while, it looked like it might be yet another rough outing for Gerrit Cole as the New York Yankees get closer to the playoffs.
Cole allowed a two-run home run to Arizona Diamondbacks superstar Corbin Carroll in the bottom of the second inning.
The Yankees had spotted Cole a five-run lead, but with the way the veteran right-hander has pitched lately, that didn't feel as safe as it potentially would've in the past.
On this Friday night, though, Cole was sharp from there. He didn't allow another run.
Cole eventually went 6.0 innings to earn a quality start, allowing four hits and those two runs while not walking any hitters. He struck out six while improving his season record to 9-9 and his ERA to 3.63.
Ryan Yarbrough, Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil polished the game off out of New York's bullpen in a 9-2 win that improved the Yankees to 89-64.
This night was about a lot of Yankees, including Ben Rice with a triple and a home run, and George Lombard Jr. with a home run as part of a five-run first.
But the most crucial thing that happened for New York was that Cole found his groove again. They'll need him sharp in the playoffs, and with only a couple more outings for him before then, this was a great step in the right direction.
Cole also made a fun bit of history in the process.
Gerrit Cole's New MLB History
Cole has now won the most games in an MLB career for any pitcher drafted No. 1 overall, according to MLB's Sarah Langs.
This was the 162nd pitching win of Cole's career.
The previous record was held by Mike Moore, who won 161 games after being the first overall pick in 1981.
David Price holds third place on the list with 157 wins after going in the top spot in 2007.
Cole can now expand on this record going forward, and considering how many fewer pitching wins starting pitchers are getting in this era, he probably has a chance to push the record out of reach if he has a few more solid seasons.
Gerrit Cole Draft
Cole was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2011 MLB Draft out of UCLA.
Four pitchers began the 2011 draft. The Mariners picked lefty Danny Hultzen out of Virginia second. The Diamondbacks chose Cole's UCLA teammate Trevor Bauer third. And the Orioles snagged high school righty Dylan Bundy fourth.
The first hitter chosen was high school outfielder Bubba Starling to the Royals at the fifth pick.
The National stook Rice slugger Anthony Rendon at No. 6.
The Diamondbacks were back on the board at No. 7 to get Archie Bradley, a high school righty.
The back-to-back picks at Nos. 8 and 9 were Francisco Lindor and Javier Baez to the Indians and Cubs, then the Padres got Cory Spangenberg at No. 11 before the Astros chose George Springer with the 11th pick.
It was a fascinating start to a draft, to be sure, with Cole living up to his hype.

New York Yankees starter Gerrit Cole made MLB history in Friday night's 9-2 win against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
The 36-year-old earned his 162nd career victory, moving past Mike Moore's 161 wins for the most ever by a pitcher who was selected No. 1 overall in the MLB Draft. Cole was chosen first by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2011, while Moore went to the Seattle Mariners with the top selection in 1981. David Price is next on the list, ranking third with 157 career wins.
The milestone came as Cole bounced back after allowing seven home runs across his previous two starts, the highest two-game figure of his career. He also had surrendered leadoff home runs in each of those outings.

After working on his delivery and potential pitch-tipping issues since his previous start against the New York Mets, Cole retired Arizona in order during a 12-pitch opening inning. Corbin Carroll later hit a two-run homer on a four-seam fastball that missed its location, but Cole gave up nothing else to the Diamondbacks.
The right-hander completed six innings, allowing two runs and four hits while issuing no walks and striking out six. He threw 90 pitches, with 62 going for strikes, finishing with a 9-9 record.
New York provided Cole with plenty of early support, sending its first five hitters to base against Eduardo Rodriguez during a five-run opening inning. Ben Rice drew a bases-loaded walk, Amed Rosario delivered an RBI single and George Lombard Jr. added a two-run single.
Rice later launched his 39th homer of the season in the third inning, while Lombard hit his own solo shot in the sixth and finished with three RBIs.
The Yankees improved to 89-64 and moved within four games of the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with nine games remaining. New York had already secured a postseason berth and has now won 11 of its last 15 games.

PHOENIX — Gerrit Cole llegó al Chase Field con mucho más en juego en su salida del viernes por la noche que el resultado final de un partido de septiembre. Los Yankees ya se habían asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el orden de su rotación aún se estaba definiendo y a Cole solo le quedaba un pequeño margen para afianzar su puesto en ella.
Los Yankees le dieron margen de maniobra desde el principio. Cole supo aprovechar bien esa ventaja para que los Yankees se llevaran una cómoda victoria por 9-2. Lanzó seis entradas, cedió cuatro hits y dos carreras, ponchó a seis y no concedió ninguna base por bolas. El as de los Yankees lanzó 62 de 90 lanzamientos como strikes y eliminó a 13 de los últimos 15 bateadores a los que se enfrentó.
Los Yankees siguieron sumando carreras y Spencer Jones echó una mano a Cole con una atrapada en deslizamiento en la tercera entrada.
Con esta victoria, los Yankees se sitúan con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y 5 1/2 partidos por delante de Boston en la lucha por la primera plaza de comodín de la Liga Americana. Dado que la serie de comodines está programada para empezar el 29 de septiembre, la última salida de Cole en la temporada regular ya no se centra tanto en acumular minutos de juego como en demostrar que la versión en la que los Yankees pueden confiar en octubre es la que está ahora en el montículo.
Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en la postemporada, pero el equipo aún tiene que organizar una rotación sólida para una serie corta, en la que una sola salida floja puede dar al traste con toda la ronda. Cole llegó a Arizona con solo una salida más, después de esta, que pudiera influir en esa decisión.
Cole alcanza un hito que ningún número 1 del draft ha logrado nunca
No fue hasta que los Yankees sentenciaron el partido cuando la noche de Cole pasó a ocupar un lugar más destacado en la historia de la MLB. Esa victoria fue la número 162 de su carrera, lo que le permitió superar a Mike Moore como el lanzador con más victorias de todos los seleccionados en el número 1 del draft de la MLB. Pittsburgh eligió a Cole como primera elección en 2011. Moore, elegido en primer lugar por Seattle en 1981, terminó con 161 victorias. David Price ocupa el tercer puesto entre los lanzadores elegidos en el número 1 del draft, con 157.
Este hito vino acompañado de una advertencia de octubre que aún pesaba. Corbin Carroll conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la segunda entrada con una bola rápida de cuatro costuras que no llegó donde debía. Fue el único daño que Arizona le hizo a Cole, pero ese lanzamiento fue importante por lo que había pasado justo antes del viernes.
Cole había encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, la mayor cantidad que había permitido nunca en un periodo de dos salidas. Cuatro de esos siete fueron con bolas rápidas de cuatro costuras. Si sumas el jonrón de Carroll, cinco de los ocho jonrones que el as de los Yankees ha encajado en sus últimas tres salidas han sido con la bola rápida de cuatro costuras.
El problema del lanzamiento de cuatro costuras se ha reducido, pero no ha desaparecido
Cole ha encajado 10 jonrones en sus últimas seis salidas, en las que ha cedido 18 carreras en 34 2/3 entradas. Su balance es de 9-9, con una efectividad de 3,63, un WHIP de 1,10 y 123 ponches frente a 22 bases por bolas en 121 1/3 entradas y 21 salidas como titular.
Antes de las malas salidas contra San Diego y los Mets, Cole tenía una efectividad de 3,29 en 18 aperturas. En las cuatro aperturas previas al viernes, los bateadores habían conseguido 16 de 48 contra su bola rápida de cuatro costuras, mientras que en sus primeras 16 aperturas habían conseguido 32 de 173 contra ella.
El as de los Yankees ha registrado una tasa de strikes fallidos del 11,6 % con su lanzamiento de cuatro costuras en las tres salidas que llevaba hasta el viernes, por debajo del 22,8 % que había logrado en sus primeras 17 salidas. Los Yankees necesitaban pruebas de que ese lanzamiento volviera a funcionar contra bateadores del nivel de la postemporada.
Boone mantiene a Cole en los planes de los Yankees para octubre
Aaron Boone ya había dejado claro que dos malas salidas no iban a dejar fuera a Cole de la rotación de los Yankees para la postemporada. Tras la derrota de los Yankees ante los Mets, Boone dejó claras sus expectativas.
«Espero que la próxima vez acierte», dijo Boone.
Lo del viernes no ha cambiado el plan general de Boone para octubre. Cuando le preguntaron si Cole debería contar con ser titular si los Yankees llegan a la Serie de Comodines, el entrenador volvió a respaldarlo.
«Sí, espero que Gerrit Cole sea el abridor», dijo Boone.
La cuestión más importante es qué versión de la bola rápida de Cole le acompañará. El analista de YES Network, David Cone, había señalado los lanzamientos secundarios, diciendo que los bateadores se habían acostumbrado a esperar la bola rápida.
«No respetan tus lanzamientos secundarios, están esperando tu bola rápida», dijo Cone.
Una salida más supone una prueba a la altura de octubre
Cole tiene prevista una salida más en la temporada regular, en casa contra los Rays la semana que viene. Esa salida puede dar a los Yankees una idea más clara antes de organizar su plantilla de lanzadores de cara a una posible serie de comodín al mejor de tres.
El viernes se dieron pasos importantes. El as de los Yankees atacó la zona de strike, no concedió ninguna base por bolas y mantuvo a raya a Arizona tras el golpe de Carroll en la segunda entrada. Además, los Yankees limitaron su carga de trabajo a 90 lanzamientos.
Pero la pregunta sobre el jonrón le siguió hasta salir del Chase Field. Cole hizo historia en la MLB y recuperó algo de confianza en la misma noche. La bola rápida de cuatro costuras aún tiene una última prueba en septiembre antes de que los Yankees decidan hasta qué punto pueden confiar en ella en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

Ben Rice hits 39th homer, Cole becomes winningest No. 1 draft pick as Yanks cruise past D-backs 9-2
Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control early and beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2
PHOENIX -- Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control early and beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 on Friday night.
After learning three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge was headed back to the injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees won for the eighth time in 10 games. New York, which has already clinched a playoff spot, is four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with nine games remaining.
The D-backs' have lost three straight and their playoff hopes are in major trouble. They're five games back of the final NL wild card with eight games left.
New York's first five batters reached against D-backs' All-Star left hander Eduardo Rodriguez and George Lombard Jr.'s two-run single made it 5-0. Lombard added a solo homer in the sixth and finished with three RBIs.
Cole (9-9) bounced back from a pair of starts that saw him surrender seven homers — the most he's ever given up over a two-game span. He gave up two runs and four hits in six innings, striking out six.
Selected first by Pittsburgh in 2011, Cole won his 162nd game. That is one more than Mike Moore, picked No. 1 by Seattle in 1981.
Rodriguez (15-7) picked a bad time to have arguably his worst start this season, needing 45 pitches to get three outs, his career high for a first inning. He gave up seven runs, five hits and four walks over 5 1/3 innings.
Corbin Carroll hit a two-run homer to cut the deficit to 5-2 in the second. Rice's solo homer in the third pushed the Yankees ahead 6-2.
The D-backs send RHP Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77 ERA) to the mound Saturday night while the Yankees counter with RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95).

item.content:encoded:
Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. Despite the Yankees’ storied franchise, only six pitchers have won the Cy Young award for the team. Schlittler is likely about to change that.
With 6.0 fWAR accumulated throughout the 2026 season, Schlittler is tied with Milwaukee Brewers’ sensation Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead among pitchers. It’s no coincidence that both hurlers are the favorites to take home the Cy Young in their respective leagues. For Schlittler, he’d not only be the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the award, but he’d also be the youngest.
As the Yankees prepare for another postseason run, they will hope that Schlittler’s historic performance is able to carry over into October. As history has taught us, the Yankees win when their pitchers win.
Yankees Complete History of Cy Young Award Winners
It’s hard to fathom that the Yankees only average a Cy Young award winner every 20 years or so. From Mike Mussina to CC Sabathia, the franchise has certainly featured plenty of Hall of Fame pitchers that have come close to winning the award. Mussina was overshadowed by teammate Roger Clemens during his stellar 2001 campaign with the Yankees. Sabathia got as close to third place in the voting following his 2010 season.
Even the great Mariano Rivera couldn’t quite do enough to sway the voters and win the elusive award as a reliever. He finished in the top three of voting four separate times. This includes two seasons when he finished in the top 10 of the MVP race. It’s rare, but pitchers have occasionally made strong cases for MVP.
We’ll detail the six previous Yankees who actually managed to cross the finish line and why they deserved to take home the top pitching award. And because a Yankees season isn’t complete without a World Series title, we’ll also note how far a Cy Young winner got the team in the postseason.
Gerrit Cole, 2023
As the most recent Yankees pitcher to win the award, Gerrit Cole did something in 2023 that only one other player had accomplished in the team’s history, winning the award by unanimous decision. With all 30 first place votes, Cole more than doubled the amount of points that second-place pitcher Sonny Gray received.
As you might imagine, Cole’s 2023 is his most impressive season with the Yankees since joining the club in 2020. He struck out 222 hitters across 209 innings pitched. Although his 3.16 FIP doesn’t scream “elite pitcher,” he allowed just 157 hits while surrendering just 48 walks.
Despite Cole’s brilliance, the club finished with a mediocre 82-80 record, missing out on the playoffs for the first time since the 2016 season, though you couldn’t blame Cole for that. He boasted a 1.03 ERA and a minuscule 0.686 WHIP over his last five starts of the season, including a two-hit shutdown against the Toronto Blue Jays in his last start of the season. If only Aaron Judge hadn't run toe-first into the wall at Dodger Stadium.
Roger Clemens, 2001
As mentioned earlier, Clemens scooped away a lot of votes from Mussina when he won the Cy Young in 2001. Some would argue that Clemens probably stole that award, but you can’t deny that he still had a very good season.
With more emphasis placed on individual wins back then, Clemens boasted 20 wins to go alongside his 213 strikeouts. Clemens’ 2001 season would probably be considered his weakest of his seven award-winning seasons. But hey, it was the early 2000s. People voted more on vibes than actual performance.
Clemens’ 3.29 FIP that season was enough to help take the Yankees to the World Series, where they lost in heartbreaking fashion to the Arizona Diamondbacks. But we don’t have to dwell on that part.
Ron Guidry, 1978
Before Clemens won the award in 2001, it had been 23 years since a Yankees pitcher won it. But oh man, did Ron Guidry ever earn the award in 1978. With a 1.74 ERA across 273 1/3 innings pitched, his season is what many consider to be the best by a pitcher in team history. His home run per nine rate of 0.4 is almost laughable.
Even by modern metrics, Guidry was the clear-cut winner that season. His 2.19 FIP and 208 ERA+ was leaps and bounds better than any other pitcher up for consideration that year, which is why he became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award unanimously.
Guidry was a large reason that the team won 100 games that year. The Yankees would carry that tremendous momentum into the postseason and defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers in the World Series.
Sparky Lyle, 1977
Unlike the long wait in between Clemens and Guidry winning the Cy Young, the Yankees actually had quite the time in the late 70s when it came to award-winning pitchers. Before Guidry, the team saw reliever Sparky Lyle take home the award in 1977. He became just the second reliever in MLB history to win the honor. Since then, seven more relievers have joined the rare club.
When looking at his numbers, you probably wouldn’t really consider Lyle to be a dominant force out of the bullpen. Despite that, he was certainly one of the most effective pitchers in the league. With just 68 strikeouts in 137 innings, Lyle didn’t just rely on swing and misses to get outs. He collected 13 wins and 26 saves, demonstrating just how pivotal he was to the Yankees.
With Lyle coming out of the pen, the Yankees won 100 games in the regular season. He then helped pave the way to a World Series title over the Dodgers.
Whitey Ford, 1961
With 236 career wins and six World Series rings in his collection, Whitey Ford is one of the foremost Yankees winners in team history. In 1961, he added a Cy Young to his trophy case. At 32 years old, he threw a career-high 283 innings, which included 11 complete games and three shutouts.
Ford’s 1961 season may be outshined in the annals of history by Roger Maris’ record-setting performance, but that doesn’t make it any less impressive. Like other pitchers on this list, Ford didn’t put up mind-boggling numbers or boast off-the-charts metrics. Outside of innings pitched, he didn’t really do one thing extremely well. However, he did do just about everything very well.
Ford was more than enough of a pitcher to be considered the ace of a team that some argue to be one of the best teams in MLB history. With 109 wins and a World Series title, it is hard to argue against that claim.
Bob Turley, 1958
Just three years before Ford won his Cy Young, Bob Turley became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award in 1958. Once again, like a number of other Yankees on this list, Turley’s 1958 season isn’t something that you would circle as an all-time great year. His 4.04 WHIP and 119 ERA+ were shockingly poor in hindsight.
Turley probably became the first Yankees pitcher to steal the award from a more deserving pitcher as well. Sorry, Warren Spahn. While Turley threw 245 1/3 innings, including 19 complete games, he was an especially wild pitcher. Turley walked 128 batters, nearly double the amount of walks surrendered by the second and third place pitchers in the Cy Young voting combined that year.
With all of that said, Turley pitched well enough to help lead the Yankees to 92 wins. They then went on to defeat the Milwaukee Braves in seven games in the World Series. When all is said and done, what more could you ask for?
